_comment: qwark's registration, to be merged into settings.json. Not loadable as-is:
settings.json has no comment syntax, so this key is here for a reader and
must not survive into the real file.
THE RULES PATH BELOW IS AN EXAMPLE. Change it to wherever you installed
the rule files. docs/INSTALLING.md walks through the whole registration.
TWO THINGS IN THE COMMAND LINE ARE LOAD-BEARING.
1. `|| exit 2` is the only fail-closed exit. Confirmed in the Claude Code
binary and its documentation: exit 0 with no JSON is NO DECISION and the
command proceeds, and any non-zero exit other than 2 is a
`non_blocking_error` and the command ALSO proceeds. Only exit 2 blocks.
So a qwark that segfaults, is killed for running out of memory, or exits
1 the way a Unix program usually reports failure, lets the command
through. qwark recovers from its own panics and runs in a single
goroutine so that it can; this catches what it cannot catch itself.
2. The rule paths are given here rather than found, so the policy in force
is readable where the hook is registered rather than implied by which
files happen to be sitting in a directory.
THE RULE FILES MUST NOT BE WRITABLE BY THE USER CLAUDE CODE RUNS AS, nor
may the directory holding them: a writable directory permits
unlink-and-replace, which defeats an unwritable file.
THE DENY LIST IS THE OTHER HALF OF qwark, AND IT IS NOT OPTIONAL.
qwark gates Bash. Write and Edit reach every path below without passing
through it, so a rule qwark enforces against a shell is enforced against
nothing at all unless the same path appears here. Keep this list in step
with the groups in rules/20-paths.toml; they are one control written twice
because two different mechanisms enforce the two halves.
WHY A TASK DEFINITION IS ON THIS LIST. An agent that can write a new file
can get the agent to approve anything. `just checks` is a fixed, familiar
command line whose meaning lives in a file in the working tree. Permitting
the command permits whatever that file says tomorrow, and no gate reading
command lines can see the difference. The executors are all denied in
rules/10-commands.toml today; if one is ever permitted, its definition file
has to be unwritable or the permission is worth nothing.
SYNTAX, read out of the Claude Code binary 2.1.233 rather than recalled:
permissions has allow, ask and deny arrays of `Tool(specifier)` strings.
Shipped examples in the binary include "Edit(//etc/*)",
"Edit(~/.claude/settings.json)" and "Bash(rm -rf *)".
`//` is an absolute path, `~/` is home, and a BARE path is relative to
the settings file root, which is the project root for project settings
and ~/.claude for user settings.
That last point splits this list in two. The absolute and ~ entries
belong in USER settings. The bare task-definition entries are relative
and belong in PROJECT settings, where they resolve against the project
root; putting them in user settings would silently mean ~/.claude/justfile
and match nothing.
SYMLINKS: RESOLVE THESE ON THE MACHINE YOU INSTALL ON. It is unverified
whether Claude Code resolves a symlink before matching, so list both
spellings where the target is known, and derive them with `readlink -f`
rather than copying somebody else's. On the machine this was written for,
~/.claude/settings.json, ~/.claude/hooks, ~/.zshrc and ~/bin all resolved
into other trees, three of the four moved within a day, and ~/.bashrc did
not exist at all. Those resolved paths are NOT shipped below; add the ones
your machine reports.
